sections.heading: Comparison

Chesky focuses on where design belongs in the process and on envisioning the ideal experience; Field focuses on design and craft as competitive differentiation and on giving a product a distinctive character.

result.question: What does Teresa Torres recommend for continuous discovery, and what does Ronny Kohavi recommend for trustworthy experiments?

answer.summary: Teresa Torres recommends building continuous customer-feedback loops and using small, prioritized assumption tests. Ronny Kohavi recommends experimentation systems that protect launches, measure outcomes, and detect problems so results can be trusted.

sections.heading: Teresa Torres: continuous discovery
sections.content: Keep customers involved as products evolve by building continuous feedback loops; interviewing customers as little as once a week can be part of that. For testing ideas, break them into underlying assumptions, prioritize those assumptions, and run small tests focused on individual assumptions. She describes teams testing multiple assumptions across several ideas in a week as a sustainable approach.

sections.heading: Ronny Kohavi: trustworthy experiments
sections.content: Treat the experimentation platform as both a safety net—so harmful launches can be aborted quickly—and an oracle that reports effects on key and other metrics. Build checks that identify problems with experiments and stop when something is wrong; trustworthy results are essential for organizational trust.

answer.summary: Before deciding, ask what is pushing you away, what progress you want from work, and whether you know where you would go next. Also examine what gives or drains your energy; a short break for reflection may help clarify what work means to you.

sections.heading: What is pushing you away?
sections.content: Ask whether several problems are adding up—not just one bad day. The discussion names feeling disrespected and no longer learning as examples of pushes that can build toward leaving.

sections.heading: What progress do you actually want?
sections.content: Ask what you hope a different job will change, beyond simply earning more. Clarify what progress means to you, and consider whether you know where you want to go; otherwise, you may land in the same or a worse situation.

sections.heading: What gives you energy, and what drains it?
sections.content: Notice which parts of work energize or exhaust you. One suggested exercise is to block off a few hours during a workday for a walk or an activity you used to enjoy, then reflect on what comes up—including any guilt and what it says about your beliefs about work.

sections.heading: If you are deciding whether to continue a startup venture
sections.content: Ask whether you still enjoy the work and spending time with your co-founders, or whether it is seriously affecting you and your relationships. This advice was given in a discussion about struggling startups, so it may be most relevant if that describes your situation.

answer.summary: April Dunford recommends identifying what a customer would do if the product did not exist: include the status quo solution, even if it is manual or imperfect, and the other options that make the customer’s shortlist.
